initial.name: Weak measure tests and quotient homeomorphism
initial.old:
The organizing idea is a single sentence.  \emph{The weak topology sees the
values of a potential and the mass of a measure; the strong topology sees,
in addition, one real number --- the energy --- and that number is exactly
what is needed to make the Monge--Amp\`ere operator a homeomorphism.}
initial.new:
Weak potential convergence records values at divisorial points; weak
measure convergence records integrals against every continuous test
function. The strong topologies also require convergence of the respective
energies. Under the standing envelope property, the Monge--Amp\`ere map
then induces a homeomorphism from potentials modulo constants to
finite-energy measures.

initial.name: Monotone theorem and independent ordered criterion
initial.old:
Let $(\phi_i)$ be a monotone net in $\mathcal E^1$ with weak limit
$\phi\in\mathcal E^1$.  Then $\phi_i\to\phi$ strongly.  If
$\phi_i\leq\phi$ for all $i$, strong convergence is equivalent to
$E(\phi_i)\to E(\phi)$.
initial.new:
Let $(\phi_i)$ be a monotone net in $\mathcal E^1$ with weak limit
$\phi\in\mathcal E^1$. Then $\phi_i\to\phi$ strongly.
For any net $(\psi_i)$ in $\mathcal E^1$ and fixed
$\psi\in\mathcal E^1$ with $\psi_i\le\psi$ for every $i$,
strong convergence to $\psi$ is equivalent to
$E(\psi_i)\to E(\psi)$; no weak-convergence assumption is needed
for this ordered criterion.

initial.name: Remove duplicated monotone sketch
initial.old:
For a decreasing net, this is continuity of energy along decreasing nets.
For an increasing net, BJ's mixed-energy continuity theorem gives energy
convergence; this is \cite[Theorem~12.5]{BJ22}.  Under
$\phi_i\leq\phi$, the tangent inequality gives

\[
 0\leq J_\phi(\phi_i)
 \leq E(\phi)-E(\phi_i),
\]

which proves the last assertion by
\Cref{thm:bj-strong-e1-quasimetric}.

initial.name: Prove ordered criterion without weak assumption
initial.old:
For the last assertion, $\phi_i\le\phi$ gives
$J_\phi(\phi_i)\le E_\omega(\phi)-E_\omega(\phi_i)$ by
\Cref{lem:ch47-IJ-elementary}\,\cref{itm:ch47-IJ:monotone}, hence
$I(\phi_i,\phi)\le(n+1)\bigl(E_\omega(\phi)-E_\omega(\phi_i)\bigr)$ by
\eqref{eq:bj-I-J-comparison}; this is \Cref{cor:ch47-monotone-I}.  If in
addition $\phi_i\to\phi$ weakly, then
$\sup\phi_i\to\sup\phi$ as in the proof of
\Cref{thm:bj-strong-e1-quasimetric}, so
$\mathbb I(\phi_i,\phi)\to0$ as soon as
$E_\omega(\phi_i)\to E_\omega(\phi)$; the converse implication is
\Cref{lem:ch48-net-criterion}\,\cref{itm:ch48-net:criterion}.
initial.new:
For the ordered criterion, the I/J comparison and monotonicity give
\[
 I(\psi_i,\psi)\le(n+1)J_\psi(\psi_i)
 \le(n+1)\bigl(E_\omega(\psi)-E_\omega(\psi_i)\bigr).
\]
Suppose the energies converge. Normalize
$u_i:=\psi_i-\sup\psi_i$ and $u:=\psi-\sup\psi$.
Translation invariance gives $\mathbb I(u_i,u)=I(\psi_i,\psi)\to0$,
so \Cref{thm:bj-strong-e1-quasimetric} gives strong convergence of $u_i$
to $u$, and hence $E_\omega(u_i)\to E_\omega(u)$. Consequently
\[
 \sup\psi_i=E_\omega(\psi_i)-E_\omega(u_i)
 \longrightarrow E_\omega(\psi)-E_\omega(u)=\sup\psi.
\]
Thus $\mathbb I(\psi_i,\psi)\to0$. Conversely, strong convergence
includes energy convergence by definition. This is
\cite[Proposition~12.6]{BJ22}.

initial.name: Polarization topology without unsupported global gauge comparison
initial.old:
Concretely, if $\omega,\omega'\in\Amp(X)$ then there is $t>0$ with
$t\omega\le\omega'\le t^{-1}\omega$, with the inequalities in the nef
order and $t$ chosen sufficiently small. The source comparison gives
comparable dual energies and strong gauges, with constants depending on the
classes. Thus the dual-energy sublevels are cofinal,
$\cM^1(\omega)=\cM^1(\omega')$, and the strong measure topologies
coincide. The potential classes themselves retain their positivity
conditions; they are not equal sets merely because both classes are ample.  What does \emph{not} survive is any numerical
statement: $E^\vee_\omega\ne E^\vee_{\omega'}$, and
$I^\vee_\omega\ne I^\vee_{\omega'}$, as
\Cref{ex:ch47-p1-numbers} already shows by varying $d$.  This is one more
instance of the rule stated in \Cref{sec:ch47-dictionary}: the class of
finite-energy objects is intrinsic, the numbers attached to them are not.
initial.new:
Concretely, choose $s\ge1$ with
$s^{-1}\omega\le\omega'\le s\omega$ in the nef order.
\cite[Theorem~9.24]{BJ22} gives comparable dual energies, so their
sublevels are cofinal. For each normalized bounded
$J_\omega$-sublevel, \cite[Lemma~9.25]{BJ22} gives a rescaled
bounded $J_{\omega'}$-sublevel containing it, and conversely.
The uniform-pairing criterion of \Cref{thm:bj-strong-measures}
therefore identifies the two strong topologies, as in the proof of
\cite[Proposition~10.16]{BJ22}.

This argument does not supply a global pointwise comparison of
$I^\vee_\omega$ and $I^\vee_{\omega'}$; that stronger comparison is
posed separately in \cite[Remark~10.17]{BJ22}.
The potential classes retain their positivity conditions and are
not equal sets merely because both classes are ample. The energies and
gauges also retain their class-dependent numerical values.
The intrinsic objects here are the set of finite-energy measures
and its strong topology.

initial.name: Distinguish sublinear capacity bound from continuity domination
initial.old:
Two further comments.  The quantitative form
\cref{itm:ch48-mvc:holder} is a genuine domination of $\mu$ by a power of
the capacity, with exponent $1/(n+1)$, and it is the trivially valued
analogue of the hypothesis in \Cref{def:ch29-capacity-domination}, where
over a discretely valued base such a domination has to be \emph{assumed}
in order to run the continuity theory.  Here it is a theorem, and the
reason is the Calabi--Yau theorem: every finite-energy measure is a
Monge--Amp\`ere measure, so the splitting of $B$ along a sublevel set of
its own potential is available.  Second, the exponent $1/(n+1)$ is not
claimed to be optimal; for $n=1$ it gives $\mu(B)\lesssim
\Capa_\omega(B)^{1/2}$, and \Cref{ex:ch48-p1-capacity} shows that no
exponent larger than $1$ can hold in general.
initial.new:
The global quantitative form gives a capacity power bound with
exponent $1/(n+1)$. It follows here by splitting the measure along
sublevels of its finite-energy Monge--Amp\`ere potential.
\Cref{def:ch29-capacity-domination} instead assumes an exponent
$1+\alpha>1$ for the discretely valued continuity argument.
The present sublinear estimate does not discharge that stronger
hypothesis.

The exponent is not claimed to be optimal. On the curve it is
$\tfrac12$. For the quartic profile in \Cref{ex:ch48-p1-capacity},
the measure of the compact ray tail $R_p^{\ge t}$ is
$(1+t)^{-3/4}$, whereas its capacity is $t^{-1}$ for $t\ge1$.
Thus even that fixed finite-energy measure admits no bound
$\mu(B)\le C\Capa_\omega(B)^q$ with $q>3/4$.
In particular a universal conclusion with exponent greater than one
cannot follow from finite energy.

initial.name: Remove duplicated compactness criterion sketch
initial.old:
Normalized psh compactness provides weak cluster subnets.  Lower
semicontinuity of $J=-E$ on the normalized locus gives the finite-energy
claim.  Criterion \eqref{eq:bj-weak-energy-strong-criterion} is precisely
the characterization of the strong topology in
\Cref{thm:bj-strong-e1-quasimetric}.  Notice that no conclusion is
drawn merely from the energies of weak cluster points: energy is upper
semicontinuous, not weakly continuous.  The last assertion is
\Cref{prop:bj-strong-monotone}.

In detail.

initial.name: Maximizer compactness requires continuous pairing
initial.old:
Two positive statements survive, and they are what the variational method
actually uses.  Energy sublevels are weakly compact, so maximizers exist
(\Cref{thm:ch47-existence-admissible}); and $\mathbb I$-Cauchy nets do
converge (\Cref{thm:ch48-completeness}), so almost-maximizing nets, which
are Cauchy by \Cref{prop:ch47-maximizing-cauchy}, converge strongly.  The
absence of strong compactness costs nothing, because in every application
the Cauchy property is available.
initial.new:
The variational method uses two separate conclusions.
For admissible data, weakly compact energy sublevels together with
continuous pairing and upper semicontinuity of the objective give
a maximizer (\Cref{thm:ch47-existence-admissible}).
For arbitrary finite-energy data, almost-maximizing nets are Cauchy
by \Cref{prop:ch47-maximizing-cauchy} and converge strongly by
\Cref{thm:ch48-completeness}. These arguments do not require
strong compactness of an entire energy sublevel.

initial.name: Thuillier domain and countability comparison
initial.old:
\emph{(6) The exact analogue in Thuillier's theory.}  This is the trivially
valued form of \cite[Remarque~3.6.12]{Thu05}, recorded in
\Cref{rem:ch25-thuillier-vs-bfj}: over a residue field of cardinality
greater than $\aleph_0$, the set of type~$\mathrm I$ points reducing to
the distinct residues of the Gauss point is closed, lies in the
$-\infty$ locus of a subharmonic function on each connected component of
the punctured space, and has infinite outer relative capacity.  In both
settings the mechanism is the same: the definition of ``polar'' or
``pluripolar'' asks for \emph{one} function, and a single psh function has
only countably many rays along which it can decrease, because the sum of
its initial slopes is bounded by the degree.  The countability clause in
\cite[Th\'eor\`eme~3.6.11]{Thu05} is thus not a technical convenience, and
neither is the appearance of $\sigma$-ideals in
\Cref{prop:ch48-pluripolar-negligible}\,\cref{itm:ch48-pn:ideal} and in
\Cref{prop:polar-sigma-ideal}.
initial.new:
\emph{(6) Comparison with Thuillier's countability warning.}
In \cite[Remarque~3.6.12]{Thu05}, choose one type-$\mathrm I$ point
for each residue class of an uncountable residue field. The resulting
set is closed in the punctured domain
$\Omega=\mathbf A^{1,\An}_K\setminus\{\zeta_{0,1}\}$ and has
$C^*(\cdot,\Omega)=+\infty$. A global negative subharmonic function
on this disconnected $\Omega$ can nevertheless have all those
points in its pole set. The set is not polar in Thuillier's definition,
which requires a countable cover by connected open domains.

The present global ample-psh example uses a different constraint:
one normalized potential on $\mathbf P^1$ has finite total initial
slope and therefore decreases on only countably many rays.
It cannot have poles at the endpoints of uncountably many rays.
Thuillier also discusses the set inside a connected open disc
containing the Gauss point, where the finite local Laplacian mass
prevents a single subharmonic pole function.
These examples explain the need to retain both the domain and the
countability signature. The relative capacity $C^*(\cdot,\Omega)$
is not identified with the global probability capacity here.
